lead: Routine calls follow one pattern, the same in every port and every language. It keeps transmissions short and tells each station when to speak. The rest is manners: the channel belongs to everyone in range.

sections.title: Who you want, who you are, OVER

qa.q: What is the correct way to call another yacht on VHF?
qa.a: Say the name of the station you are calling, then **THIS IS**, then your own name, and end with OVER. Say each name once, or twice when reception is poor; three times is for distress, urgency and safety.

blocks.p: A call has three parts in a fixed order: the **name of the station you are calling**, the words **THIS IS**, and **your own name**. Say each name once, or twice when reception is poor; three times is for distress, urgency and safety calls. You end with **OVER**.

fig.title: Calling a yacht on 16
lines: Blue Star, Blue Star, Blue Star,

blocks.p: To answer a call, turn it round: the caller's name, THIS IS, your name, OVER. "Blue Star, this is Aurora, OVER."
If you do not know a vessel's name, describe her so that she recognises herself, by type and position: "Motor yacht anchoring north of me in Vathi Bay, this is Aurora, OVER."

sections.title: Meet on 16, talk on a working channel

qa.q: After making contact on channel 16, how do I switch to a working channel?
qa.a: Propose an intership **working channel** digit by digit, "channel seven two", confirm the agreed one in a word and switch. On the new channel listen first, then call the station again before your message.

blocks.p: On 16 you only make contact. As soon as the other yacht answers, you propose an intership working channel, digit by digit: "channel seven two". She may propose another one instead. Whichever is agreed, confirm it in a word and switch.

fig.title: Aurora and Blue Star
lines: 16 · Aurora, this is Blue Star, OVER
16 · Aurora, this is Blue Star, seven two
72 · Blue Star, this is Aurora, OVER
72 · Aurora, this is Blue Star, OVER

blocks.p: On the new channel listen for a moment to make sure it is free, then call the station again before you give your message. If she does not come up after a call or two, go back to 16, where you last had contact, and call her once more.

qa.q: Is it correct to say "over and out" on the radio?
qa.a: No, the two never go together: **OVER** means you have finished and expect a reply, OUT that the exchange is finished and no reply is expected. "Over and out" asks for a reply and refuses it.

blocks.p: Only one station can speak at a time, so every transmission ends with a word that says what comes next.

head: Word
Means
Then
rows: I have finished and I expect your reply
the exchange is finished, no reply expected

blocks.p: The two never go together: "over and out" asks for a reply and refuses it in one breath. When the other station ends with OUT, say nothing more.

blocks.rule: OVER: your turn. OUT: we are done. Never both.

sections.title: A short call on their own channel

qa.q: How do I ask a marina for a berth on the VHF?
qa.a: Call it on its own working channel, not 16, with a short call, and wait for the answer. Then give the whole request in **one message**: the boat, her length, how many nights.

blocks.p: A marina or a port authority is called on its own working channel, the one in the pilot book, not on 16. Make a short call and wait for the answer. Then give the whole request in one message: the boat, her length, how many nights.

fig.title: Asking for a berth
lines: Vega Marina, this is Aurora, OVER
Aurora, this is Vega Marina, OVER
Vega Marina, this is Aurora, a berth
Aurora, berth B 14, stern to, OVER
Berth B 14, stern to, thank you, OUT

blocks.p: When a station calls you, answer that station and give exactly what it asked for. A port authority that asks for your name and intentions hears: "Port Authority, this is Aurora, mooring at the town quay, OVER."

qa.q: What should I do if nobody answers my VHF call?
qa.a: Wait a few minutes before calling again. If the station is far off or behind a cape, try later, when you are closer, not more often: **radio discipline** keeps the channel usable for everyone in range.

list: **Listen before you transmit.** If others are talking, wait until they finish; never talk over them.
**Low power in port.** 1 W reaches the fuel dock across the marina and does not block the channel for boats miles away.
**Keep it short.** One message with everything in it: others are waiting to call.
**No answer?** Wait a few minutes before you call again. If the station is far off or behind a cape, try later, when you are closer, not more often.
**Nothing private.** Everyone in range hears you: no card numbers on the air.
**No needless transmissions.** Channel 16 stays clear for distress and calling, and the radio is not a toy.

blocks.rule: Listen, think, then press: short, clear, and off the air.
